Iran’s president says U.S. memorandum is best path out of war
-    Click here to listen to this article

- Iran’s president said the June memorandum of understanding with the U.S. remains the best path out of the current state, which he called ‘neither war nor peace.’
- With Iran’s economy squeezed by sanctions and a U.S. naval blockade, Pakistan’s army chief heads to Tehran in the latest effort to defuse tensions and revive stalled negotiations.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Sunday defended the memorandum of understanding signed with the United States in mid-June as the best way to move beyond a situation of “neither war nor peace.”
“There is not a single provision in this agreement that amounts to capitulation,” Pezeshkian said in a speech published by state-run IRNA early Sunday. “The supreme leader sets the policies, and we will follow that path.”
The memorandum of understanding opened a 60-day period for talks aimed at ending the war and reaching an accord on Iran’s nuclear program. That period ended last week with no signs of compromise, especially on the crucial issue of reopening the Strait of Hormuz, vital to global shipping. The strait had been an open, international waterway before the war.
Pezeshkian said his country can’t attract investment in this stalled phase. Nearly six months after the war began, Iran’s economy is suffering under sanctions and a U.S. naval blockade.
Pakistan’s army chief to visit Tehran
Pakistani Field Marshal Asim Munir will lead a delegation to Tehran on Monday, Iranian state television reported, citing Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei.
Two regional officials said the visit was part of Islamabad’s efforts to de-escalate tensions between the United States and Iran and urge them to return to the negotiating table. The officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly.
Iranian protester executed
The Iranian judiciary’s Mizan news agency reported the latest execution connected to nationwide antigovernment protests early this year, saying Majid Adineh was arrested Jan. 9 in Mohammadshahr, west of Tehran.
The judiciary said forensic examinations indicated the handgun found on him had been fired on Jan. 8 and Jan. 9. Mizan said Adineh had joined the protest following calls by groups opposed to Iran’s government and alleged that he had received training from groups outside the country.
A Revolutionary Court in Karaj convicted Adineh under Iran’s law imposing harsher penalties for espionage and cooperation with hostile states. Mizan said the verdict accused him of carrying out operations on behalf of Israel, the United States and groups Iran considers hostile.
Prior to the latest execution, Iran had executed at least 56 people on national security-related charges since mid-March, including 27 in cases linked to the pro-democracy protests, United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk said in a report issued early this month.
“I am alarmed by the rise in executions and death sentences issued in Iran since March and that capital punishment continues to be used to instill fear among the population and suppress dissent,” Turk said in the report.
Israeli teen settler arrested in beating of amputee
Elsewhere in the Middle East, police arrested a 16-year-old boy from the Israeli settlement of Avigayil in the beating of a 61-year-old Palestinian man. Saeed Muhammad Ibrahim Rabah was struck with a pipe outside his home in the occupied West Bank, a year after he lost a leg after being shot by a settler.
Rabah told the Associated Press that two settlers arrived at his home in Khirbet al-Rakeez on Saturday afternoon. One struck him on his back when he approached, Rabah said. He called the violence an effort to make families leave.
“We will remain, no matter what happens,” he said after filing a police report. “This is our land and this is our homeland, and we must protect it.”
Separately, the Palestinian Health Ministry in the West Bank said a 14-year-old in the Askar refugee camp in Nablus was shot dead by Israeli forces, which did not immediately comment. Nehad Ajouri, uncle of the victim, Islam Maher Ajouri, called the shooting indiscriminate.
Also in the West Bank, Israel’s military said it had detained a suspect in a stabbing attack that wounded a 24-year-old Israeli man in the area of Al-Auja. Israel’s emergency services said the man was taken to a hospital and was in “moderate” condition.
Airstrike in Gaza kills a 4-year-old
Four-year-old Mohammed Taha died after an Israeli airstrike hit a house in central Gaza on Sunday, hospital authorities said. The strike in Zawaida also wounded at least five other people, including a child, according to the Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital, which received the casualties.
The military later said it struck and killed a Hamas commander in central Gaza. Al-Aqsa Martyrs Hospital confirmed that the man named in the statement, Ismail Abu Ful, was killed.
An Israeli strike in southern Gaza wounded at least seven people, including three children, according to health officials at Nasser Hospital. The military did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Also, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz in a statement said he instructed the military to “act immediately and forcefully” to prevent launches of balloons, kites or drones from Gaza toward nearby Israeli communities.
“We view every launch as an act of war in every respect,” he said.
Before the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas-led militants on Israel — when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage — burning kites and balloons were sent from Gaza into southern Israel, causing fires and other damage.
While the heaviest fighting has subsided since a fragile ceasefire in the Israel-Hamas war took hold in October, Israeli forces have carried out repeated airstrikes, killing more than 1,280 Palestinians, according to health officials in Gaza.
The Gaza Health Ministry, part of the Hamas-led government, maintains detailed casualty records that are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It doesn’t give a breakdown of civilians and militants.

Iran: President defends US deal as best option for peace
August 23, 2026
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian on Sunday defended Tehran's expired Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with the United States as the best option for ending hostilities between the two nations, which Pezeshkian described as being "neither war nor peace."
Pezeshkian said members of Iran's Supreme National Security Council (SNSC) agreed with the assessment on the basis of, "dignity, wisdom and national interest."
"There is not a single provision in this agreement that amounts to capitulation," Pezeshkian said in remarks published by state-run news agency IRNA. "The supreme leader sets the policies, and we will follow that path."
The MoU, signed by US President Donald Trump in June, laid out a 60-day timeline for ending the US-Israeli-led conflict as well as ensuring that Iran give up its nuclear ambitions.
The deadline passed last week with no signs of compromise by either side, and the situation in the Strait of Hormuz — which Iran closed in response to US-Israeli attacks, putting the global economy in a chokehold for the past six months — still unresolved.
On Sunday, Pezeshkian called it imperative that Iran exit this stalled phase of the conflict to unlock foreign investment to the country.
"Capital and money are extremely sensitive to risk," he said. "We have to remove this risk from the country."
Pakistani mediator expected in Tehran as hardliner warns neighbors not to help US
Iran's Foreign Ministry on Sunday announced that Pakistan's top military leader, Asim Munir, will travel to Iran on Monday.
The visit is part of "Pakistan's ongoing efforts to help consolidate peace and security in the region," Tehran said.
Pakistan was instrumental in getting the MoU between Washington and Tehran signed.
Earlier this month, Islamabad signed its own regional security cooperation agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, which observers read as an attempt to counter Iranian influence in the region.
Still, despite news of Munir's travels and Pezeshkian's announcement that the SNSC backs the MoU, that body's new hardline leader, Mohsen Rezaei, warned neighboring countries against aiding the US war effort, saying, "If [Trump] wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner."

He described the situation as a “full-scale economic, military and security war”, as Iran faces mounting pressure from US measures and restrictions on its trade.

Iran has also warned countries against supporting the US campaign. Mohsen Rezaei, the new head of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, threatened retaliation if countries friendly to Tehran were targeted by US measures.

By yourNEWS Media Newsroom.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian defended his government’s memorandum of understanding with the United States on Sunday, arguing that the agreement offers Iran its best chance to escape a costly state of “neither war nor peace” nearly six months into its conflict with the United States and Israel.
His comments came as Tehran’s newly appointed top security official delivered a significantly more confrontational message, warning neighboring countries that Iran could attack their interests and alternative Persian Gulf oil-shipping routes if they participate in additional U.S. economic measures against the Islamic Republic.
Pezeshkian said members of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council had concluded that the memorandum represents the strongest agreement presently available when measured against Iran’s national interests and principles of dignity and wisdom.
“There is not a single provision in this agreement that amounts to capitulation,” Pezeshkian said in remarks published early Sunday by the state-run IRNA news agency. “The supreme leader sets the policies, and we will follow that path.”
President Donald Trump signed the Memorandum of Understanding in June, establishing an ambitious 60-day timetable for ending the war and reaching an agreement concerning Iran’s nuclear program.

The new head of Iran’s top security body warned Sunday that Tehran will see any country’s support for new U.S. economic measures against the Islamic Republic as an “act of war,” while Iran’s president defended a memorandum of understanding with the United States as the best way out of the stalled conflict.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Monday is expected to announce the new measures after the U.S. vowed to impose an “unprecedented” level of economic warfare and isolation on a country that has lived for decades under sanctions. Also Monday, Pakistan’s army chief is expected to visit Iran as mediators try to revive talks.
Meanwhile, attacks calmed on the Strait of Hormuz but posturing did not, as a recently created Iranian authority listed dozens of vessels it said will face restrictions on future transits.

Iran’s security chief sharpens warning to neighbors
The hard-line leader of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, issued his latest warning on X, with the comments quickly shared by Iranian state media.
It came a day after Rezaei’s most extensive public comments since being named to the post this month.
“If (Trump) wants to do something, we will retaliate in a seismic manner,” he had told the state broadcaster in an interview that aired late Saturday. He said Iran would target other oil-shipping routes from the Persian Gulf — alternatives to the Strait of Hormuz.
Rezaei, a former Revolutionary Guard commander and military adviser to Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, was part of senior appointments widely seen as hardening Tehran’s political and military stance.
Iranian president wants to move past ‘neither war nor peace’
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian earlier Sunday said the memorandum of understanding signed in mid-June was the best way to move beyond a situation of “neither war nor peace,” adding that Tehran can’t attract investment nearly six months after the war began.
“There is not a single provision in this agreement that amounts to capitulation,” Pezeshkian said in a speech published by state-run IRNA. “The supreme leader sets the policies, and we will follow that path.”
The interim deal opened a 60-day period for talks aimed at ending the war and reaching an accord on Iran’s nuclear program. That period ended last week with no signs of compromise or extension.
No attacks confirmed on the strait, but new restrictions
There were no confirmed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz over the past 48 hours, a multinational coalition overseen by the U.S. Navy said Sunday, with shipping traffic still at reduced levels. The U.S. military said its blockade of Iranian ports had redirected 70 commercial ships and disabled three as of Sunday.
Iran’s recently created Persian Gulf Strait Authority, sanctioned by the U.S., published a list of dozens of ships it said had violated arrangements for transiting the strait and would face future restrictions like fines or seizures. Before the Oct. 7, 2023, attack by Hamas-led militants on Israel — when 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage — burning kites and balloons were sent from Gaza into southern Israel, causing fires and other damage.
Hamas in a statement Sunday accused Israel of “using children’s toys as a pretext” for attacks and further displacement of Gaza residents.
